unit.title: Follow principles of Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) in work environment

summary: This unit teaches you to work safely and keep others safe in a workshop or on site. You will learn the duties of employers and workers, how to spot hazards and judge risks, the order of controls, how to choose and look after PPE, what safety signs mean, how to work safely with machines, electricity, gas cylinders, chemicals, noise, heat, manual handling and ladders, how to keep the workplace tidy, what to do in a fire or other emergency, basic first aid, and why every accident and near miss must be reported.

blocks.p: This unit is shared by several programmes, including Welding and Electrical Installation. **Occupational health and safety (OH&S)** means protecting people at work from injury and ill health. Workshops and sites are full of hazards: electricity, hot metal, sparks, gas cylinders, fumes, noise, heavy steel, sharp edges, ladders, chemicals and the Jamaican heat. Most accidents happen because a hazard was not noticed, or was noticed and ignored.

Safety is not only for the supervisor. Every trainee and worker must look out for hazards, follow the rules, use the protection provided, and report what is wrong. This unit gives you the habits that every other unit in your programme expects.
**Who it is for:** Level 2 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and new workers in any workshop or on any site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Know your duties and rights
Follow the safety rules, use PPE, look out for others, report hazards, and stop and report work that is unsafe; know what your employer must provide.
Spot hazards and judge risks
Find hazards in your area and task, decide who could be harmed, and rate the risk as low, medium or high.
Control risks
Choose controls in the right order, from removing the hazard down to PPE.
Use PPE and safety signs
Choose, check, wear and look after the right PPE; understand every kind of safety sign.
Work safely with equipment and substances
Machines and guards, hand and power tools, electricity and safe isolation, gas cylinders, chemicals and their SDS, fumes, dust, noise and heat.
Handle, lift and climb safely
Lift and carry safely, get help or a lifting aid, and use ladders and steps correctly.
Keep the workplace tidy
Keep walkways and exits clear, run cables safely, clean up spills, and put waste in the right bins.
Respond to emergencies
Raise the alarm, use the right extinguisher only when it is safe, evacuate, and give basic first aid.
Report
Report hazards, accidents and near misses at once and help record them.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on hazards and risk, controls, PPE, signs, fire, emergencies, electricity, first aid, reporting, manual handling, housekeeping, chemicals, gas cylinders, ladders, machines, rights and duties, and health and welfare.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as OH&S, PPE, RCD, CPR, arc eye, hot work permit, fire drill, accident book and flammable) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: a hazard inspection and risk assessment of a work area, and an evacuation drill with basic first aid (cooling a burn and the recovery position). The assessor watches how you behave as well as what you write.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, workplace safety has long been covered by the Factories Act and its regulations, enforced by the Occupational Safety and Health Department of the Ministry of Labour and Social Security. A wider occupational safety and health law has been in preparation for some years. Your instructor will tell you which law is in force now; this kit teaches the good practice that all of them expect.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Health and safety works only when everyone plays their part. The employer (or the training centre) provides a safe place and safe ways of working; the worker (or trainee) works safely and looks out for others.

head: The employer must
The worker must
rows: Provide a safe workplace, with safe machines, tools and electrical installations that are checked and maintained
Carry out risk assessments and put controls in place
Provide the right PPE free of charge, and replace it when it is worn out
Give information, training, a safety induction and supervision
Provide first aid, fire-fighting equipment, safe exits and emergency procedures
Provide welfare: clean toilets, washing facilities and drinking water
Record and investigate accidents
Take care of their own safety and that of anyone affected by their work
Follow the safety rules, procedures and training
Wear and look after the PPE provided
Use machines and tools only as trained and authorised
Never misuse or interfere with safety equipment, guards or signs
Report hazards, faults, accidents and near misses
Stop and report a task they believe is unsafe

ul: **To know:** to be told about the hazards of your work and how you are protected.
**To take part:** to raise safety concerns and to take part in safety meetings or a safety committee.
**To stop unsafe work:** if you believe a task is dangerous, stop, tell your supervisor why, and do not start again until it has been made safe. Good employers welcome this.

blocks.p: Every new worker or trainee gets a **safety induction** before starting: the hazards of the workplace, the rules, the PPE, where the exits, extinguishers, alarm points, first-aid kit and assembly point are, who the first-aiders are, and how to report problems. If you have not had one, ask for it.

ul: Never come to work under the influence of alcohol, ganja (cannabis) or other drugs. They slow your reactions and judgement.
Tell your supervisor if you are taking medicine that makes you drowsy.
Tiredness causes accidents: get enough sleep, and take your breaks.
No horseplay: pushing, joking with tools or air lines, and playing with gas or electricity have killed people.
Keep your phone away while you work with machines, heat or electricity.

blocks.note: Report it, do not ignore it. A hazard you walk past is a hazard you have accepted. Telling your supervisor is not getting anyone into trouble; it is how hazards are fixed before someone is hurt.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **hazard** is anything that could cause harm: a live cable, a spinning grinder disc, an oily floor, a gas cylinder, a heavy plate. A **risk** is **how likely** it is that the hazard will cause harm, together with **how bad** the harm could be. A hazard with a high risk needs action first.

head: Type
Examples in a welding shop or on an electrical job
rows: Physical
Heat, noise, arc light (UV), sun, vibration from tools, poor lighting
Mechanical
Rotating discs, drills and lathes; flying chips; sharp edges; falling or rolling steel
Electrical
Live parts, damaged leads, wet conditions, overloaded outlets, overhead lines
Fire and explosion
Sparks and hot metal, gas cylinders, fuel, paint and thinners, oily rags
Chemical
Welding fume, zinc fume, solvents, paints, cleaners, cement and silica dust
Biological
Mosquitoes breeding in standing water, rat urine (leptospirosis), dirty toilets, mould
Ergonomic (manual handling and posture)
Heavy lifting, awkward bending, kneeling, overhead work, repeated movements
Working at height
Ladders, roofs, platforms, open edges and holes
Psychological
Stress, long hours, tiredness, bullying

blocks.p: Many workplaces rate risk with a simple matrix: score how likely harm is and how bad it would be, then multiply.

head: Likelihood ↓ / Severity →
1 Minor (first aid only)
2 Serious (time off work)
3 Major (permanent injury or death)
rows: 1 Unlikely
1 Low
2 Low
3 Medium
2 Possible
2 Low
4 Medium
6 High
3 Likely
3 Medium
6 High
9 High

blocks.p: Example: a damaged welding lead lying in a puddle where people walk. A shock is **likely** (3) and could kill (3), so the score is 9: **high**, deal with it now. A small offcut at the edge of a bench is unlikely to cause more than a cut finger: **low**, but still tidy it away.

blocks.h: The steps of a risk assessment

flow: Look at the task and the area, and list the hazards
Decide who could be harmed and how: the worker, others nearby, visitors, the public
Rate the risk: low, medium or high
Choose controls, following the order of controls
Write it down and tell everyone involved
Review it when something changes, after an accident or near miss, or at set times

blocks.p: Choose controls from the **top** of this list down. The higher the control, the better it works, because it does not depend on people remembering to do the right thing. **PPE comes last**: it protects only the wearer, and only if it is the right kind, in good condition and worn properly.

head: Control
What it means
Welding example
Electrical example
rows: 1. Elimination
Remove the hazard altogether
Have steel cut to size by the supplier, so there is no cutting in the shop
Work dead: isolate the circuit so there is nothing live to touch
2. Substitution
Replace it with something less dangerous
Use a water-based paint instead of one with a strong solvent
Use battery tools instead of mains tools outdoors
3. Engineering controls
Separate people from the hazard by physical means
Fume extraction at the bay; guards on the grinder; welding screens
RCD or GFCI protection; panel covers; barriers
4. Administrative controls
Change the way people work
Hot work permits, training, signs, safe work procedures, rotas to limit time in noise
Lock-out and tag-out procedures, permits, warning signs, supervision
5. PPE
Protect the person
Helmet, gloves, leather apron, safety boots, ear protection
Safety boots, safety glasses, insulated gloves where required

blocks.note: Often you use several controls together: extraction (engineering), a hot work permit (administrative) and a respirator (PPE). Start at the top and work down until the risk is as low as you can make it.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Body part
PPE
When
rows: Head
Hard hat; flame-resistant cap under a welding helmet
Where things can fall or you can strike your head; under a welding helmet against sparks
Eyes and face
Safety glasses with side shields; goggles; face shield; welding helmet or goggles with the right filter
Always in the workshop; a face shield over safety glasses for grinding; the correct filter for welding and cutting
Ears
Ear plugs or ear muffs
Grinding, cutting, hammering, chasing walls: whenever noise is loud
Lungs
Dust mask or respirator of the right type, fitted properly
Dust, fume or vapour that extraction does not remove
Hands
Leather gauntlets; cut-resistant gloves; chemical gloves; insulating gloves where required
Matched to the hazard: heat, sharp edges, chemicals, electricity
Feet
Safety boots with toe caps and good soles
Always in the workshop and on site
Body
Flame-resistant cotton overalls; leather apron; high-visibility vest on sites with vehicles
Matched to the work
Falls
Harness and lanyard, as trained
Work at height where guardrails cannot be used

ul: **Check PPE before each use.** Cracked lenses, torn gloves, a damaged hard hat or a worn strap may not protect you.
Make sure it fits. A loose respirator lets dust past the seal.
Clean it and store it properly, out of the sun and away from chemicals.
Report damaged or worn-out PPE and get it replaced. Never alter it.
Wear it every time, even for a quick job.

blocks.note: Sunglasses do not protect against arc light, and a paper dust mask does not stop welding fume or chemical vapour. **Arc eye** (welder's flash) is a painful burn to the eye from looking at an arc without the right filter; it often starts hours later. Screens round welding bays protect the people nearby.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Kind of sign
Shape and colours
Meaning
Examples
rows: Prohibition
Red circle with a red line across it, black picture, white background
You must not
No smoking; no naked flames; do not use mobile phones
Mandatory
Blue circle with a white picture
You must
Wear eye protection; wear ear protection; wear safety boots
Warning
Yellow triangle with a black border and black picture
Danger: take care
Danger, high voltage; flammable material; hot surface
Safe condition
Green square or rectangle with a white picture
The way to safety, or safety equipment
Emergency exit; first aid; eyewash; assembly point
Fire equipment
Red square or rectangle with a white picture
Where fire-fighting equipment is
Fire extinguisher; fire alarm call point; fire hose

blocks.p: Signs are an administrative control: they warn and instruct, but they do not remove the hazard. Never cover, move or ignore a sign, and report one that is damaged or missing.

sections.title: Machines, tools, electricity and gas cylinders

ul: Use a machine only when you have been trained and your supervisor allows it.
**Guards** stop hands, clothing and flying pieces reaching the dangerous parts. Never remove or bypass a guard; if one is missing or damaged, do not use the machine, and report it.
Tie back long hair; do not wear loose clothing, rings, chains or watches near rotating machines. They can be caught and pull you in.
Know where the stop button or the isolator is before you start.
Never leave a machine running unattended, and wait for it to stop before you clear chips or adjust it.
Use hand tools in good condition: no loose hammer heads, mushroomed chisels or cracked handles.
Check that the disc or wheel is the right type, rated for the machine's speed, and not cracked or damaged.
Keep the guard on and, on a bench grinder, the eye shield in place and the **tool rest close to the wheel** (about 3 mm or less), so work cannot be dragged in between.
Stand to one side when you start a grinder, and let it run for a moment before use.
Wear safety glasses and a face shield, ear protection and gloves suited to the job.
Point sparks away from people and from anything that can burn. Unplug the grinder before you change a disc.
Check plugs, leads and tools before use: no cracked casings, bare wire, burn marks or split sheaths. Take damaged items out of use, label them and report them.
Do not overload outlets or plug power strips into each other.
Run leads where they cannot be tripped over, crushed or soaked.

Use **RCD or GFCI** protection for portable tools, especially outdoors and in wet places. An RCD cuts off the supply quickly when current leaks to earth (usually at 30 mA; a GFCI outlet at about 5 mA).
Keep water away from electrical equipment, and never touch equipment with wet hands.
Only trained, authorised people work on electrical installations.

blocks.h: Safe isolation before work on a circuit or machine

flow: Identify the right circuit or machine and its isolator or breaker; tell the people affected
Switch off and isolate
Lock it off with your personal lock and keep the key; fix a tag saying who is working and that it must not be switched on
Check your voltage tester on a known live source or a proving unit
Test at the point of work, between all the conductors, to prove it is dead
Check the tester again on the known source
Only then start work; remove your lock only when the work is finished and safe

blocks.note: Never work on live equipment. If the tester fails its check, the "dead" reading means nothing: stop and get a working tester.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Screen the welding bay so that arc light and spatter do not reach other people.
Before welding or cutting near anything that can burn, remove it or cover it with a fire-resistant blanket, and keep an extinguisher ready.
Where welding or cutting is done outside the normal welding area, a **hot work permit** is usually needed: written approval that the area has been checked and made safe.
Keep a fire watch during the work and for a time afterwards, as the workplace's rules say.
Store cylinders **upright and chained** (or in a cylinder trolley), in a cool, well-aired place, away from heat, sparks, fuel and oil.
Keep oxygen away from oil and grease: oil in oxygen can burst into flame. Never use oil on oxygen fittings or handle them with oily gloves.
Keep acetylene cylinders upright at all times.
Close the valves when the cylinders are not in use, and keep the valve caps on cylinders in store.
Store full and empty cylinders apart, and mark empties.
Check hoses and connections for leaks with soapy water, never a flame. Make sure flashback arrestors are fitted.
Move cylinders on a trolley; never roll them on their sides or lift them by the valve.

sections.title: Chemicals, fumes, dust, noise, heat and health

blocks.p: Paints, thinners, degreasers, cleaners, adhesives, resins, gases and many other products can burn the skin and eyes, harm the lungs, poison, or catch fire. Their containers carry **hazard pictograms** (a black symbol on a white diamond with a red border), and each product has a **safety data sheet (SDS)**, which gives its hazards, the PPE to wear, first aid, safe storage, and what to do with spills and fires.

head: Pictogram shows
Meaning
rows: A flame
Flammable: catches fire easily (petrol, thinners, acetylene)
A flame over a circle
Oxidiser: makes fires burn fiercely (oxygen)
Liquid dripping onto a hand and a metal bar
Corrosive: burns skin and eyes, and attacks metal
A skull and crossbones
Toxic: can kill in small amounts
An exclamation mark
Harmful or irritant: can irritate the skin, eyes or lungs
A person's outline with a star on the chest
Serious long-term health hazard, such as cancer or lung damage
A gas cylinder
Gas under pressure
A dead tree and fish
Harmful to the environment

ul: Keep chemicals in their **original, labelled containers**. Never put them in drink bottles: someone may drink them.
Store them in a cool, well-aired store, away from heat, sparks and the welding bay; keep flammables in a flammables cabinet.
Keep lids on, use only what you need, and clean up spills at once as the SDS says.
**Never mix** cleaning chemicals: some mixtures, such as bleach with acid or ammonia cleaners, give off poisonous gas.
Wash your hands before eating, drinking or smoking.
Welding, cutting, soldering and solvents give off fumes and vapours that harm health. Use **ventilation and extraction** close to the source, and keep your head out of the fume.
Galvanised (zinc-coated) steel gives off zinc fume when welded or cut, which causes metal fume fever. Remove the coating from the work area and use extraction.

Cutting, grinding or chasing concrete, block and stone makes fine **silica dust**, which scars the lungs over time. Use tools with dust extraction or water, and wear a dust mask of the right type (such as FFP3 or N95), properly fitted.
Old paint may contain lead: ask before grinding or burning it off.
Grinding, cutting, hammering and chasing walls are loud enough to damage your hearing. The damage builds up slowly, does not hurt, and is permanent.
A rule of thumb: if you have to shout to be heard by someone about 2 m away, wear ear protection.
Ringing in the ears after work is a warning sign.
Use quieter tools and methods, keep noisy work away from others, and wear ear plugs or muffs.

blocks.p: Jamaica's heat, especially from May to October, makes heat illness a real hazard, worse in full PPE, on roofs and beside hot work.

head: Condition
Signs
What to do
rows: Heat exhaustion
Heavy sweating, pale and clammy skin, dizziness, headache, feeling sick, weakness, cramps
Move the person to a cool, shaded place and let them lie down
Loosen or remove heavy PPE and clothing
Give sips of cool water
Cool the skin with wet cloths and a fan
Watch them; call 110 if they do not improve quickly or get worse
Heat stroke (an emergency)
Confusion, slurred speech, strange behaviour, collapse or fits; very hot skin, which may be dry
Call 110 at once
Cool them fast: shade, wet cloths, fanning, cool water on the skin
Recovery position if unconscious but breathing; CPR if not breathing

ul: Drink water often, before you feel thirsty. Sugary and energy drinks do not replace water.
Take breaks in the shade, and plan heavy work for the cooler hours of the day where you can.
Do not take off PPE to keep cool: find shade, rest and drink instead.
Outdoors, wear a hat or hard hat with a brim where allowed, and long sleeves.
**Mosquitoes** that carry dengue, chikungunya and Zika breed in clean standing water: in old drums, tyres, buckets, tarpaulins and blocked gutters. Empty, cover or remove anything that holds water.
**Leptospirosis** comes from rat urine in water and mud. Keep food waste covered, keep the workplace free of rubbish where rats live, cover cuts, and wash your hands.
**Welfare:** clean toilets, washing facilities, drinking water and a clean place to eat are part of a safe workplace. Do not eat where you work with lead, chemicals or fume.

blocks.p: Back injuries are among the most common injuries at work. There is no weight that is safe for everyone. Guide figures used in many countries are about 25 kg for a man and 16 kg for a woman, lifted close to the body at waist height, and much less when the load is held away from the body, lifted from the floor or above the shoulders, or lifted often. If in doubt, get help or use a lifting aid.

flow: Plan: check the weight, size and grip; check the route is clear and there is space to put the load down
If it is too heavy or awkward, get help or a trolley, hoist or other lifting aid
Stand close to the load, feet apart, one foot slightly forward
Bend your knees, keep your back straight, and get a firm grip
Lift smoothly with your legs, keeping the load close to your body
Do not twist: turn by moving your feet; make sure you can see over the load
Put it down by bending your knees, then adjust its position

ul: **Team lifts:** agree one person to give the commands; lift, carry and put down together. Carry long bars and tubes with a person at each end, on the same shoulder.
Wear gloves against sharp edges and safety boots against dropped loads.
Use a ladder only for short, light work. For longer work, use a platform or scaffold put up by a competent person.
Check it before use: stiles straight, rungs firm, feet in place, no cracks.
For electrical work, use a **non-conductive** (fibreglass or wooden) ladder, never aluminium.
Set a leaning ladder at about **1 out for every 4 up** (about 75°). A ladder reaching 4 m up a wall has its foot about 1 m out.
Stand it on firm, level ground; tie it at the top or have someone foot it.
If you step off at the top, the ladder should stick out about 1 m (three rungs) above the landing.
Keep **three points of contact** (two feet and a hand) while you climb; carry tools in a belt or haul them up.
Do not overreach: keep your belt buckle between the stiles. Move the ladder instead.
Never stand on the top three rungs of a leaning ladder or the top two steps of a stepladder, unless it has a platform and handrail made for it.
Look up for overhead power lines before you raise a ladder.

blocks.p: **Good housekeeping** means keeping the work area clean, tidy and organised all the time, not only at the end of the day. It prevents slips, trips and falls, cuts from sharp metal, and fires from sparks landing on rubbish, and it keeps the escape routes open.

ul: Put tools back in their places after use.
Keep walkways, stairs and exits clear; never block a fire exit, an extinguisher or the main switch.
Run cables and hoses along the edges or cover them; never through puddles or under closed doors.
Clean up spills of oil, water or chemicals at once, or fence them off and report them.
Put offcuts, stubs and scrap in the right bins; do not leave sharp offcuts on benches.
Keep oily and solvent-soaked rags in a **metal bin with a lid**, and empty it regularly.
Stack materials safely, not too high, with heavy items low.

blocks.p: A fire needs three things: **heat, fuel and oxygen**. Take any one away and the fire goes out. Water cools (removes heat); a fire blanket or CO2 smothers (removes oxygen); shutting off a gas valve removes the fuel.

ul: Keep things that burn away from hot work and sparks; remove or cover them before welding or cutting.
Store flammable liquids and gas cylinders correctly, away from heat.
Do not overload electrical outlets; report damaged leads and burning smells.
Keep oily rags in a closed metal bin; keep rubbish from piling up.
Keep a fire watch after hot work.

head: Extinguisher
Use it on
Never use it on
Notes
rows: Water
Wood, paper, cardboard, cloth
Live electrical equipment; burning oil, fuel or cooking fat
Cools the fire well, so solids do not flare up again
Foam
Burning liquids such as petrol, thinners and paint; also wood and paper
Live electrical equipment
Forms a blanket over the liquid
Carbon dioxide (CO2)
Live electrical equipment; burning liquids
Not suited to wood, paper and cloth: it does not cool, so they can flare up again
The horn gets extremely cold; the gas can make breathing hard in a small room
Dry powder (ABC)
Most kinds of fire, including electrical
Cooking fat fires
Makes a mess and makes it hard to see; can damage electronics
Wet chemical
Cooking oil and fat fires
Electrical equipment
Found in kitchens
Fire blanket
A small pan fire; a person whose clothes are on fire
Large fires
Smothers the fire by cutting off the oxygen

blocks.p: Always **read the label**: it shows the kinds of fire the extinguisher is for. Labels use letters for classes of fire, but the letters differ: on American-standard extinguishers, common in Jamaica, **C** means live electrical equipment; on British and European ones, C means flammable gas, and electrical fires are shown by a symbol. Go by the pictures and words, not the letter alone.
Use an extinguisher the **PASS** way: **P**ull the pin, **A**im at the base of the fire, **S**queeze the handle, **S**weep from side to side.

flow: Raise the alarm: shout "Fire!" and set off the fire alarm
Call the fire brigade on 110 and give the address and a landmark
Fight the fire only if it is small, you are trained, you have the right extinguisher, the alarm has been raised, and your way out is behind you
If it is safe, switch off the electricity and close gas cylinder valves
If the fire grows, or the extinguisher does not put it out quickly, get out at once and close the doors behind you (do not lock them)
Go to the assembly point and answer the roll call; never go back in for belongings

ul: Know the exits, the alarm call points and the **assembly point** for your area.
Leave by the nearest safe exit. Walk, do not run; do not use a lift.
In smoke, **keep low**, where the air is cleaner, and feel closed doors with the back of your hand before opening them: a hot door means fire behind it.

At the assembly point, a **roll call** checks that everyone is out. If someone is missing, tell the fire officers or the person in charge at once. Nobody goes back in until the fire brigade says it is safe.
Tell the fire officers about gas cylinders, fuel or chemicals inside.
**Fire drills** are planned practices so that everyone knows what to do. Take them seriously.

blocks.note: Jamaica's hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. Before a storm, secure or bring in loose sheets, steel and equipment that wind could throw, switch off and protect electrical equipment, and know the workplace's plan. After a storm, watch for fallen power lines, flooded equipment and damaged structures, and report them before work restarts.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Know who the trained **first-aiders** are and where the **first-aid kit**, the eyewash and any AED (defibrillator) are kept.
The first-aid kit holds dressings, plasters, bandages, gloves, eyewash and a list of contents. If you use the last of anything, tell the person in charge so that it is restocked.
Do only what you are trained to do, and always get help.

head: Number
Service
rows: Ambulance and fire brigade
Police

blocks.p: When you call, say **who** you are, **what** has happened (for example an electric shock, a fall, a burn), **where** you are, with the address and a landmark, how many people are hurt, and whether they are breathing. Send someone to meet the ambulance at the gate.

flow: Danger: make sure it is safe for you to approach
Response: speak loudly and tap their shoulders
Shout for help; send someone to call 110 and the first-aider
Airway: tilt the head back and lift the chin
Breathing: look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds
Breathing normally: recovery position. Not breathing normally: CPR if you are trained

ul: **Do not touch** the person while they may still be in contact with the supply: you would be shocked too.
Switch off at the switch, plug or isolator. If you cannot, stand on something dry and push them or the cable clear with something dry that does not conduct, such as a wooden broom handle.
Call 110, check breathing, and give CPR or use the recovery position as needed.
Cool any burns. Everyone who has had a shock must see a doctor, even if they feel fine.
Cool the burn under **cool running water for 20 minutes**. Do not use ice.
Remove rings and watches near the burn before it swells, unless they are stuck to the skin. Do not pull off clothing that is stuck.
Cover with **cling film** or a clean, non-fluffy dressing.
Never put on butter, oil, toothpaste or creams, and never burst blisters.
Get medical help for burns bigger than the casualty's hand, burns to the face, hands, feet or groin, deep burns, and all electrical and chemical burns.
Chemical burns: brush off any dry chemical, then rinse with plenty of running water; check the SDS.

**Chemical in the eye:** rinse at once with clean running water or eyewash, holding the eyelids open, for at least 15 minutes or as the SDS says, then get medical help. Take the label or SDS with you.
**Dust or a chip:** do not rub. Rinse with eyewash; if it does not come out, or the chip is stuck, cover the eye and get medical help.
**Arc eye:** do not rub; tell the first-aider; see a doctor or nurse.

blocks.p: Wear gloves. Press firmly on the wound with a clean dressing and keep pressing; raise the injured part if you can. Do not pull out anything stuck in the wound: press around it. Get medical help for deep cuts and heavy bleeding.

flow: Kneel beside the person, who is lying on their back
Place the arm nearest you at a right angle to their body, palm up
Bring the far arm across their chest and hold the back of that hand against their near cheek
Bend the far knee up, with the foot flat on the ground
Pull on the bent knee to roll them towards you onto their side
Tilt the head back so the airway stays open, and adjust the top leg so the hip and knee are at right angles
Keep checking their breathing until help arrives

blocks.p: **CPR** (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) keeps blood moving when the heart has stopped. A trained person gives 30 hard, fast chest presses in the centre of the chest (about 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 a minute), then 2 rescue breaths, and repeats. If you are not trained in rescue breaths, give chest presses without stopping. If an AED arrives, switch it on and follow its instructions.

head: Report
Examples
rows: Accident or incident
Anyone hurt; a fire; equipment damaged
**Near miss**: an event that could have caused harm but did not
A ladder slips but nobody falls; a cylinder topples; a grinding disc shatters behind the guard
Hazard or unsafe condition
A missing guard, a damaged lead, a blocked exit, an empty first-aid kit, a used extinguisher

ul: Report **at once** to your instructor or supervisor, and write it in the **accident book** or on the workplace's form as soon as possible.
Reports let the cause be found and fixed before someone else is hurt. A near miss is a warning: next time the same cause may injure someone.
Reports also make sure the injured person gets proper care, and give a true record for the employer, insurers and, after a serious event, the authorities.

A good report gives the date, time and exact place; the names of the people involved and of witnesses; what happened, in order; the injury and the first aid given; the equipment involved; and what was done to make the area safe. It sticks to facts, not blame, and is signed and handed to the supervisor.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what OH&S means and list the main duties of the employer and of the worker.
I can explain my rights, including stopping and reporting work I believe is unsafe.
I can explain the difference between a hazard and a risk, and name the types of hazard.
I can carry out a simple risk assessment and rate a risk as low, medium or high.
I can list the order of controls, with an example of each, and explain why PPE comes last.
I can choose, check, wear and care for PPE.
I can say what each kind of safety sign means from its shape and colour.
I can work safely with machines, guards and grinders.
I can check electrical equipment and describe safe isolation.
I can store and handle gas cylinders safely and explain a hot work permit.
I can read hazard pictograms, use an SDS, and store chemicals safely.
I can control fumes, dust and noise, and prevent and treat heat illness.
I can lift and carry safely and use a ladder correctly.
I can keep my work area tidy and explain how housekeeping prevents accidents.
I can explain the fire triangle and choose the right extinguisher.
I can raise the alarm, evacuate, and go to the assembly point.
I can call for help on 110 and give the right information.
I can rescue a person from a low-voltage electric shock safely, cool a burn and place a person in the recovery position.
I can report accidents, near misses and hazards, and say what a report should include.

terms: The book or form in which accidents at work are recorded
A painful burn to the eye from an arc's UV light; also called welder's flash
The agreed place where everyone gathers after leaving the building
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest presses and rescue breaths for a person whose heart has stopped
Removing a hazard altogether; the best control
A planned practice of leaving the building
Heat, fuel and oxygen: the three things a fire needs
A person at work trained to give first aid
Catches fire easily, like petrol or thinners
Written approval needed before welding or cutting where it is not normally done
Keeping the work area clean, tidy and organised
Disconnecting equipment from its supply so it cannot be switched on
Locking an isolator off with a personal lock and fixing a tag, so nobody can switch it back on
An event that could have caused harm but did not
Elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, PPE
Residual current device: cuts off the supply quickly when current leaks to earth (a GFCI is the American equivalent)
Lying a breathing, unconscious person on their side so the airway stays open
How likely harm is, and how bad it could be
A careful check of a task to find hazards, judge risks and choose controls
The safety briefing a new worker gets before starting
Safety data sheet: the hazards of a substance and how to handle it
Replacing a hazard with something less dangerous
An instrument used to prove that a circuit is dead before work starts

c1.title: A Monday walk-round in a Yallahs fabrication yard
c1.text: During a Monday morning walk-round at a fabrication shop in Yallahs, St Thomas, the supervisor, Miss Patrice Ellis, and trainee Davian find: an oxygen cylinder standing loose beside the grinding bench, with a can of petrol next to it; the bench grinder's tool rest set about 10 mm from the wheel and its eye shield missing; offcuts of flat bar lying on the walkway near the cut-off saw, as they are most days because there is no scrap bin there; and a welding lead with a split outer cover running through a puddle by the door.

c2.title: Rewiring a house in Constant Spring
c2.text: Brianna and Rojae, Level 2 electrical trainees, are helping electrician Mr Clive Bryan rewire an old house in Constant Spring, St Andrew. Today they must chase (cut grooves in) a concrete wall for conduit with an angle grinder fitted with a masonry disc, and fit a new light on a ceiling about 3 m high, using the house owner's 2 m stepladder. The kitchen circuit has been isolated and locked off by Mr Bryan.

c3.title: A fire in the welding shop in Port Maria
c3.text: At a training centre in Port Maria, St Mary, sparks from Kevaughn's cutting torch land in a cardboard box of packing and a wooden pallet left in a corner of the welding shop, and a small fire starts. The nearest extinguishers are a water extinguisher and a CO2 extinguisher. The welding machines in the bays are switched on, but none is near the fire.

c4.title: Heat on a roof in Annotto Bay
c4.text: Sheldon and his team are welding a steel roof frame for a church hall in Annotto Bay, St Mary, on a hot August afternoon. Sheldon, in full welding PPE, has been working on the scaffold platform since 11 a.m. and has drunk only one soft drink. At 2 p.m. he climbs down and says he feels dizzy and sick and has a headache. He is sweating heavily and looks pale.

c5.title: The maintenance store at a hotel in Runaway Bay
c5.text: Renée has just started as a maintenance worker at a hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann. In the maintenance store she finds paint thinners poured into an unlabelled juice bottle on the bench, and a supervisor's note: "Use the strong drain cleaner on the kitchen drains; add bleach if it's slow." The drain cleaner's label shows a black picture of liquid dripping onto a hand and onto a metal bar, inside a red-bordered diamond.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with the oxygen cylinder and the petrol can?
o: Lay the cylinder down flat so it cannot fall, and leave the petrol where it is
Close the cylinder valve, then leave both, as a closed cylinder is safe
Chain the cylinder upright in store; move the petrol to the flammables store
Move the petrol can to the other side of the grinding bench, out of the sparks
questions.why: Oxygen makes any fire burn fiercely, and grinding sparks can ignite petrol vapour. Cylinders are stored upright and chained, away from heat and fuel, and flammable liquids go in their own store.

questions.q: Why is the bench grinder dangerous, and what should happen to it?
o: Work can jam in the gap; take it out of use until it is put right
The wheel will wear out faster; use it gently until the next service
The gap lets sparks out; wear a face shield and carry on using it
The shield only keeps dust off the wheel; reset the rest and use it
questions.why: With a wide gap, work can be dragged between the rest and the wheel, trapping fingers or shattering the wheel. The rest is reset close to the wheel (about 3 mm or less) and the eye shield refitted before anyone uses it.

questions.q: Davian rates the split welding lead lying in the puddle. Which rating fits best?
o: Low, because a welding machine's voltage is too low to hurt anyone
Medium, because the lead is only split in its outer cover
High, because a shock is likely and could kill someone
Low, because people can simply step over the puddle
questions.why: Water and a damaged lead make a shock likely, and a shock can be fatal, so the risk is high and is dealt with at once: switch off, take the lead out of use, and dry the area. A welding machine's open-circuit voltage can kill, especially in wet conditions.

questions.q: Offcuts end up on the walkway most days because there is no scrap bin at the saw. Which control is best?
o: Put up a sign by the saw telling people to watch their step
Tell everyone working in the yard to wear their safety boots
Paint yellow lines along the edges of the walkway to mark it
Put a scrap bin beside the saw and clear the walkway now
questions.why: A bin at the saw removes the cause, so offcuts stop reaching the walkway. Signs, lines and boots are lower controls that leave the trip hazard in place.

questions.q: Chasing the concrete wall makes thick dust. Which set of controls is best?
o: Dust extraction or water, a fitted FFP3 or N95 mask, others kept away
A cloth tied over the nose and mouth, and the windows opened afterwards
Safety glasses only, as concrete dust is harmless once it settles
A paper dust mask, and the dust swept up with a dry broom at the end
questions.why: Concrete dust contains silica, which scars the lungs over time. Controlling dust at the source with extraction or water comes first, then a properly fitted mask of the right type; dry sweeping puts the dust back in the air.

questions.q: On the 2 m stepladder, Rojae can reach the 3 m ceiling only by standing on the top step. What should he do?
o: Stand on the top step while Brianna holds the stepladder steady
Put the stepladder on a table to gain the extra height he needs
Get taller steps or a platform, so he stays off the top steps
Lean the closed stepladder against the wall and climb it
questions.why: Standing on the top steps leaves nothing to hold and makes the ladder tip. The right height of steps or a platform lets him work with three points of contact. For electrical work, the steps should be non-conductive.

questions.q: While the grinder runs, Brianna has to shout for Rojae to hear her from about 2 m away. What does this tell them?
o: The grinder needs a new disc, as a sharp disc runs almost silently
Only the person using the grinder needs to protect their ears
Noise is a problem only if their ears hurt at the end of the day
The noise is likely to damage hearing, so both need ear protection
questions.why: Having to shout to be heard at about 2 m is a sign the noise is loud enough to damage hearing. The damage is painless and permanent, and it affects anyone close by, not only the operator.

questions.q: The fire is small and nothing electrical is involved. Which extinguisher is the better choice for the burning cardboard and pallet?
o: The CO2 extinguisher, as it works well on every kind of fire
The water extinguisher, keeping the jet away from the machines
Both together, aimed at the top of the flames to knock them down
Neither: pull the burning box out into the yard by hand
questions.why: Water cools burning wood and cardboard so they do not flare up again; CO2 does not cool, so solids can reignite. The jet is aimed at the base of the fire, kept away from the live welding machines.

questions.q: Before Kevaughn uses the extinguisher, what must be true?
o: The fire brigade has arrived and has given him permission
Alarm raised, he is trained, and his way out is behind him
He has collected his bag and tools so he can leave quickly
Every welding machine in the shop has been unplugged first
questions.why: Fight a fire only if it is small, the alarm has been raised, you are trained, you have the right extinguisher and your escape route is behind you. If it grows, get out and close the door.

questions.q: The fire spreads and the building is evacuated. At the assembly point, one trainee is missing from the roll call. What should the instructor do?
o: Send two trainees back inside quickly to look for the missing person
Wait ten minutes, as the missing trainee has probably gone home
Go back inside alone, as the instructor knows the building best
Tell the fire officers at once where the trainee might be
questions.why: The roll call exists to find out who may still be inside. The fire officers have the equipment and training to search; anyone else who goes back in may become a second casualty.

questions.q: What should Sheldon's workmates do first?
o: Give him an energy drink and let him rest on the scaffold
Move him into shade, loosen his PPE and give him sips of water
Tell him to take off his gloves and carry on welding more slowly
Pour iced water over his head and send him back up straight away
questions.why: These are signs of heat exhaustion. Cooling him in the shade, loosening heavy PPE and clothing, and giving sips of cool water usually bring recovery; he stops work and is watched closely.

questions.q: Which sign would show that Sheldon's condition has become heat stroke, so that 110 must be called at once?
o: He says he is thirsty and asks for more water
His shirt is wet through with sweat
He wants to sit down in the shade
He becomes confused and his speech is slurred
questions.why: Confusion, strange behaviour, slurred speech, collapse or fits, often with very hot skin, mean heat stroke: a medical emergency. Call 110 and cool him fast while you wait.

questions.q: Which change to the team's plan would best prevent heat illness tomorrow?
o: Let the team take off their welding jackets when it gets hot
Ask everyone to work faster so the job finishes before noon
Hard work in cooler hours, with shade, water and rest breaks
Buy energy drinks for the team to drink instead of plain water
questions.why: Planning the hottest work for cooler hours, providing shade, water and rest breaks controls the heat without removing PPE. Rushing adds to the strain, and sugary drinks do not replace water.

questions.q: What is the main danger of the thinners in the unlabelled juice bottle?
o: Someone may drink it, and nobody can tell what it is
The plastic bottle will melt within an hour and spill the thinners
The thinners will evaporate and lose their strength more quickly
Juice left in the bottle will spoil the thinners for painting
questions.why: Chemicals in drink bottles are a well-known cause of poisoning. With no label there is no warning, and no way to find the right first aid or SDS. It goes back into a labelled container in the flammables store.

questions.q: What does the pictogram on the drain cleaner warn of?
o: It is flammable and can catch fire very easily in heat
Corrosive: it burns skin and eyes and attacks metal
It is harmful to fish and plants if it is spilled
It is a gas stored under pressure in its container
questions.why: Liquid dripping onto a hand and a metal bar is the corrosion pictogram. Wear the gloves and eye protection the SDS names, and keep it off skin and metal fittings.

questions.q: Why should Renée not follow the note to add bleach?
o: Bleach would make the drain cleaner work too fast and splash
Mixing cleaning chemicals can give off a poisonous gas
Bleach only works on surfaces, never inside drains
The hotel would be charged twice for the chemicals used
questions.why: Some mixtures, such as bleach with acid or ammonia products, release poisonous gases such as chlorine. Never mix chemicals; follow the SDS, and tell the supervisor the note is unsafe.

questions.q: Some drain cleaner splashes into Renée's eye. What is the right first aid?
o: Rub the eye gently with a clean cloth to wipe the chemical out
Put in eye drops from the first-aid kit and wait to see if it improves
Rinse it with clean water for at least 15 minutes; get medical help
Rinse it quickly, cover it with a pad and go back to work
questions.why: A corrosive keeps burning until it is washed away, so rinse at once, holding the eyelids open, for at least 15 minutes or as the SDS says. Then get medical help and take the label or SDS.

questions.q: What does a red square sign with a white picture of an extinguisher mark?
o: The place where a fire extinguisher is kept
An area where fire extinguishers must not be used
A room where there is a high risk of fire
The route to follow to the assembly point
questions.why: Red squares and rectangles show the location of fire-fighting equipment. A no-entry or not-allowed sign is a red circle with a bar, a warning is a yellow triangle, and escape routes are green.

questions.q: Two trainees must carry a 6 m length of 100 × 50 RHS across the yard. Which is the safest way?
o: One person carries it alone, balanced at the middle on one shoulder
Drag it along the ground by one end so that nobody has to lift it
Each lifts their own end when ready and walks at their own pace
One at each end, same shoulder, one person calling the lift
questions.why: A team lift with one person giving the commands means the load is lifted, carried and put down together. A long bar on one person swings into others, and dragging damages the steel and can twist the back.

questions.q: Old tyres and open drums of rainwater lie behind a workshop in Spaldings. Which health hazard do they create?
o: Mosquitoes breed in them and can spread dengue
The rubber gives off fumes that cause arc eye
The rainwater makes the workshop floor slippery
The drums attract lightning during thunderstorms
questions.why: The mosquitoes that spread dengue, chikungunya and Zika breed in clean standing water in containers. Empty, cover or remove anything that collects water.
